quizzes.title: Key terms and ideas
quizzes.intro: Ten quick checks on debtors, creditors, deferrals, accruals and the three inventory methods.

questions.q: Trade debtors (accounts receivable) arise from…
options: Sales on open account, not evidenced by a written promise
Sales backed by a signed bill
questions.explain: Accounts receivable are open-account sales. A written promise makes it a bill receivable; deposits from customers are creditors and long-term loans to associates are investments.

questions.q: A bill receivable differs from a trade debtor because it is…
options: Evidenced by a written promise to pay
questions.explain: Bills receivable are debts with written evidence; open-account debtors have none. Both are current assets, not investments.

questions.q: A long-term loan given to an associated organisation is classified as…
questions.explain: The lecture separates short-term loans (to employees, as debtors) from long-term loans to associated organisations, which are investments.

questions.q: A deferred expense, such as rent paid a year in advance, is shown as…
options: An expense of the month it was paid
questions.explain: The benefit belongs to later periods, so the prepayment is an asset (Prepaid Rent 550 after January). Only the month used becomes expense.

questions.q: An accrued expense — wages earned by workers but not yet paid — is…
questions.explain: An accrual has accumulated but is unpaid; accrued expenses are liabilities. Accrued incomes, by contrast, are assets.

questions.q: Income received in advance that is still unearned is a liability.
questions.explain: Deferred incomes are liabilities: the business owes the customer either the goods or the money back until the income is earned.

questions.q: Under FIFO, the inventory left at year end consists of…
questions.explain: FIFO sells in the order of purchase, so the oldest goods go first and the newest remain. LIFO leaves the earliest purchases.

questions.q: Inventories are always valued at…
options: The higher of cost or net realisable value
The lower of cost or net realisable value
questions.explain: The rule is the lower of cost or net realisable value, so a loss in value is recognised at once but a gain is not anticipated.

questions.q: Under LIFO the closing inventory is made up of the earliest purchases.
questions.explain: LIFO issues the newest units first, so what remains is the oldest layer — in the lecture, the 300 units of opening inventory worth 1,800.

questions.q: An advance received from a customer for fabric not yet delivered is classified as…
questions.explain: Deposits or advances from customers are listed among creditors: the business owes delivery. It becomes sales only when the goods are supplied.

quizzes.title: Formulas and relationships
quizzes.intro: The cost-of-goods-sold identity, prepayments and the direction in which each inventory method pushes profit.

questions.q: Cost of goods sold is calculated as…
questions.explain: Goods available (opening + purchases) less what is still unsold (closing stock) is what was sold. Adding closing stock reverses the formula.

questions.q: The ‘value of goods available for sale’ is…
options: Closing stock + cost of goods sold − purchases
questions.explain: Goods available = opening balance + purchases during the period (50,000 in the lecture’s worksheet). It is then split between COGS and closing stock.

questions.q: If closing inventory is stated Rs 10,000 higher, with everything else unchanged…
questions.explain: Higher closing stock means less of the goods available is counted as sold, so COGS falls and gross profit, net profit and capital all rise by 10,000 — the lecture’s three-column table shows exactly this.

questions.q: When purchase prices are rising, LIFO reports the lowest profit of the three methods.
questions.explain: LIFO charges the newest, dearest units to COGS (5,400 against FIFO’s 4,700), so profit and tax are lowest.

questions.q: The weighted average cost per unit is found by…
options: Averaging the prices of the purchase lots
Total cost of goods available ÷ total units available
Cost of the latest purchase ÷ its units
questions.explain: 7,200 ÷ 1,000 units = 7.20. A simple average of the lot prices ignores the different lot sizes.

questions.q: Rent of Rs 600 is paid on 1 January for the whole year. What is the Prepaid Rent balance at the end of March, after three months have been used?
questions.explain: Monthly rent = 600 ÷ 12 = 50. Prepaid after three months = 600 − 3 × 50 = Rs 450.

questions.q: With rising prices, which method gives the highest closing inventory value?
questions.explain: FIFO leaves the latest, highest-priced purchases in stock (2,500 against LIFO’s 1,800 and the average’s 2,160).

questions.q: Which figure in the profit and loss account does the lecture call a judgement rather than a fact?
questions.explain: Sales, purchases and expenses are facts; the value placed on goods still on the shelf is a judgement — and it moves profit rupee for rupee.

questions.q: Net sales are Rs 300,000 and cost of goods sold Rs 120,000. What is the gross profit?
Switching from FIFO to LIFO changes the number of units counted in the year-end stock take.
questions.explain: The physical count (300 units) is the same under every method; only the rupee value attached to those units changes.

quizzes.title: Worked calculations
quizzes.intro: Compute cost of goods sold, prepayments, accruals and inventory values under FIFO, LIFO and weighted average.

questions.q: Opening supplies were Rs 8,000, purchases Rs 42,000 and closing supplies Rs 13,000. What is the cost of goods sold?
Lots: 1 Jan 300 units at Rs 6; 10 Feb 300 at Rs 7; 2 Oct 300 at Rs 8; 20 Dec 100 at Rs 9. 300 units are counted at year end. What is the closing inventory value under FIFO?
questions.explain: FIFO keeps the latest purchases: 100 × 9 = 900 plus 200 of the October lot at 8 = 1,600, total Rs 2,500.

questions.q: Using the same four lots (300 at Rs 6, 300 at Rs 7, 300 at Rs 8, 100 at Rs 9) and 300 units counted, what is the closing inventory value under LIFO?
questions.explain: LIFO keeps the earliest layer: 300 × 6 = Rs 1,800.

questions.q: Goods available were 1,000 units costing Rs 7,200 in total and 300 units remain. What is the cost of goods sold under the weighted average method?
questions.explain: Average cost = 7,200 ÷ 1,000 = 7.20; units sold = 700; COGS = 700 × 7.20 = Rs 5,040.

questions.q: Insurance of Rs 2,400 for twelve months is paid on 1 March. What is the prepaid insurance asset at 30 June, after four months have been used?
Workers earn Rs 1,500 per day and four days’ wages are unpaid at month end. What accrued wages liability should be recorded?
questions.explain: Accrued wages = 1,500 × 4 = Rs 6,000, a liability until paid.

questions.q: Net sales Rs 300,000; goods available for sale Rs 140,000; closing inventory Rs 30,000; expenses Rs 40,000. What is the net profit?
A mill bought yarn in three lots: 500 kg at Rs 400, 300 kg at Rs 420 and 200 kg at Rs 450 per kg. 400 kg remain. What is the closing stock value under FIFO?
questions.explain: FIFO keeps the newest: 200 × 450 = 90,000 plus 200 kg of the middle lot at 420 = 84,000, total Rs 174,000.

questions.q: With the same three lots (500 kg at Rs 400, 300 kg at Rs 420, 200 kg at Rs 450) and 400 kg remaining, the LIFO closing stock value is…
questions.explain: LIFO keeps the oldest layer: 400 × 400 = Rs 160,000. Rs 174,000 is FIFO and Rs 166,400 is the weighted average.

questions.q: Same lots: 500 kg at Rs 400, 300 kg at Rs 420, 200 kg at Rs 450; 400 kg remain. What is the closing stock value under the weighted average method?

quizzes.title: Applied in practice
quizzes.intro: Costing-office decisions about prepayments, accruals, advances and which stock value to report.

questions.q: Cotton prices have risen all year and a mill wants to report the lowest taxable profit. Which inventory method achieves this?
options: Any — the physical count is the same
questions.explain: Rising prices make LIFO charge the dearest cotton to COGS, giving the lowest profit and tax. FIFO gives the highest.

questions.q: A mill pays its annual fire-insurance premium on 1 July. How should the premium be treated in the accounts at 31 December?
options: Entirely as an expense of the year
Half as expense, half as a prepaid (deferred) asset
Half as expense, half as an accrued liability
questions.explain: Six months’ benefit belongs to the next year, so that half is deferred as an asset; only the six months used is expense.

questions.q: The electricity used by a dyeing plant in December is billed and paid in January. In December’s accounts it should be…
options: Recorded as an accrued expense and a liability
questions.explain: The cost has accumulated but is unpaid — an accrual. It is charged to December and shown as a liability at month end.

questions.q: A customer pays Rs 500,000 in advance for a fabric order to be delivered next month. How should the mill record the receipt?
questions.explain: The income is unearned until delivery, so it is a deferred income — a liability. Recording it as sales would overstate this month’s profit.

questions.q: A canteen that physically uses up its oldest food first must also use FIFO in its accounts.
questions.explain: The physical flow and the accounting assumption are separate; the lecture notes that LIFO may be chosen ‘in harmony with inflation’ even where goods move first-in, first-out.

questions.q: Closing stock of 300 units has a FIFO cost of Rs 2,500 but, after a fall in the market, can only be sold for a net Rs 2,100. At what value should it be carried?
questions.explain: Lower of cost or net realisable value: 2,100 is below cost, so the stock is written down to Rs 2,100. The average of the two has no basis.

questions.q: An accountant overstates closing inventory by Rs 5,000 to impress the bank. Which statement is true?
options: This year’s profit is understated by 5,000
This year’s profit is overstated by 5,000 and next year’s understated by 5,000
Only the balance sheet is affected
questions.explain: A high closing stock cuts this year’s COGS; the same figure becomes next year’s opening stock and raises next year’s COGS, so the profit is only shifted, not created.

questions.q: A weaving mill had opening grey-fabric stock of Rs 1,200,000, bought Rs 6,500,000 of grey fabric during the year and holds Rs 1,450,000 at year end. What was its cost of goods sold?
A mill pays a dyer Rs 200,000 in advance for processing next month. In the mill’s own books this is…
questions.explain: Advances and deposits with suppliers are listed under debtors — the dyer owes the mill a service. It becomes expense when the dyeing is done.

questions.q: Yarn bought at Rs 450 per kg can now be sold for only Rs 380 per kg net. For the year-end balance sheet the mill should…
options: Keep it at Rs 450 since that is the cost
Write it down to Rs 380 per kg
Value it at the average, Rs 415
questions.explain: Net realisable value (380) is below cost, so the lower figure is used and the loss is taken now.

quizzes.title: Challenge review
quizzes.intro: Harder questions on the interaction between stock valuation, profit, capital and the timing of expenses.

questions.q: Goods available for sale cost Rs 7,200 (1,000 units). Under FIFO the 300 units left are valued at Rs 2,500. What is the FIFO cost of goods sold?
questions.explain: COGS = goods available − closing stock = 7,200 − 2,500 = Rs 4,700.

questions.q: If purchase prices had been falling through the year, which method would report the lowest profit?
questions.explain: With falling prices the newest units are the cheapest; FIFO leaves them in stock, so its closing inventory is lowest and its COGS highest. The usual ‘LIFO lowers profit’ rule reverses.

questions.q: FIFO closing stock is Rs 2,500 and LIFO closing stock Rs 1,800. By how much does FIFO profit exceed LIFO profit?
questions.explain: Both methods start from the same 7,200 of goods available, so the profit difference equals the difference in closing stock: 2,500 − 1,800 = Rs 700. Sales are the same under both.

questions.q: In the lecture’s example the weighted-average cost of goods sold (5,040) lies between the FIFO (4,700) and LIFO (5,400) figures.
questions.explain: The average cost of 7.20 lies between the oldest (6) and newest (9) prices, so the average method’s result falls between the two extremes.

questions.q: Rent of Rs 600 for the year is paid on 1 January. At 30 April, how much is still shown as the Prepaid Rent asset?
questions.explain: Four months at 50 = 200 has become expense; 600 − 200 = Rs 400 remains prepaid.

questions.q: A mill forgets to accrue a Rs 20,000 electricity bill for December. The effect on December’s accounts is…
options: Profit overstated by 20,000 and liabilities understated by 20,000
No effect, since the bill will be paid in January
questions.explain: The expense is missing, so profit is too high; the unpaid bill is a liability that is not shown. Paying in January does not change December’s cost.

questions.q: Other assets are Rs 200,000, closing inventory is stated at Rs 25,000 and liabilities are fixed at Rs 30,000. What capital will the balance sheet show?
Why do FIFO, LIFO and the average method all begin from the same Rs 7,200?
options: Because the tax authority fixes it
Because goods available for sale is a fact; only its split between COGS and closing stock is a judgement
Because all three methods value stock at the latest price
questions.explain: Opening stock plus purchases is recorded from invoices. The methods differ only in which units are assumed to remain.

questions.q: Which of the following is an accrual rather than a deferral?
options: Rent paid a year in advance
Interest earned on a bank deposit but not yet received
An advance received from a customer
Insurance premium paid for the coming year
questions.explain: Interest that has accumulated but not been received is an accrued income (an asset). The other three are deferrals — payments or receipts made before the period they belong to.

questions.q: Purchases were 400 units at Rs 10, then 400 at Rs 12, then 200 at Rs 15. 700 units were sold. What is the cost of goods sold under LIFO?
questions.explain: LIFO issues the newest first: 200 × 15 = 3,000, then 400 × 12 = 4,800, then 100 × 10 = 1,000; total Rs 8,800.
